units.title: Hello, Go!
units.summary: Write your first Go program and print text and numbers with fmt.Println and fmt.Printf.

lesson.md: Every Go program is made of **packages**. A program that you can run uses `package main` and has a function called `main`. Go starts the program there.

Line by line: `package main` says that this file belongs to the main package. `import "fmt"` loads the `fmt` package, which can print text. `func main()` defines the function where the program starts. Its code goes between the braces `{` and `}`.
`fmt.Println` prints its values, puts a space between them and ends the line. Text goes in double quotes, numbers do not. `fmt.Println()` without values prints an empty line.

lesson.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println("Go", "is", "fun")
    fmt.Println(1, 2, 3)
    fmt.Println()
    fmt.Println("Done")
}

lesson.md: Go can calculate for you. `2 + 3` without quotes is a calculation, but `"2 + 3"` in quotes is only text. Use `*` to multiply and `/` to divide.

lesson.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println(2 + 3)
    fmt.Println("2 + 3")
    fmt.Println(7 * 6)
}

lesson.md: `fmt.Printf` prints a **format string** and fills in values. Each verb is a placeholder: `%s` for text, `%d` for a whole number and `%v` for any value. `Printf` does not end the line, so you add `\n` (a new line) yourself.

lesson.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Printf("%s is %d years old.\n", "Ada", 36)
    fmt.Printf("%v, %v and %v\n", "text", 42, true)
    fmt.Printf("One line. ")
    fmt.Printf("Same line.\n")
}
lesson.output:
Ada is 36 years old.
text, 42 and true
One line. Same line.

lesson.md: Go is strict about tidy code. If you import a package and do not use it, the program does not compile. A line that starts with `//` is a comment, and Go ignores it.

The opening brace `{` must be on the same line as `func main()`. Go ends lines with an invisible semicolon, so a brace on the next line is an error. Go is also case sensitive: `Println` works, `println` from `fmt` does not.

card: `package main` + `func main()` make a runnable program
`fmt.Println(a, b)` prints with spaces and a new line
`fmt.Printf("%s %d %v\n", s, n, x)` fills in values

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables, get to know int, float64, string and bool, and convert between types.

lesson.md: A **variable** stores a value under a name. With `var` you write the name, the type and the value: `var age int = 13`.

lesson.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var name string = "Gopher"
    var age int = 13
    fmt.Println(name, age)
}

lesson.md: Inside a function you usually write the short form `:=`. Go finds the type from the value. To change a variable later, use `=`. `count++` adds 1, `count--` subtracts 1, and `count += 10` adds 10 (there are also `-=` and `*=`).

lesson.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    city := "Lisbon"
    count := 3
    count = count + 1
    count++
    count += 10
    fmt.Println(city, count)
}

lesson.md: `:=` creates a **new** variable, so you can use it only once per name. Go also refuses to compile a program with a variable that is declared but never used.
The most common types are `int` (whole numbers), `float64` (decimal numbers), `string` (text) and `bool` (`true` or `false`). The verb `%T` in `Printf` prints the type of a value.

lesson.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    n := 42
    price := 9.99
    word := "hi"
    ok := true
    fmt.Printf("%T %T %T %T\n", n, price, word, ok)
}

lesson.md: A variable without a value gets the **zero value** of its type: `0` for numbers, `""` (the empty string) for `string` and `false` for `bool`. The verb `%q` prints a string in quotes, so you can see the empty string.

lesson.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var i int
    var f float64
    var s string
    var b bool
    fmt.Println(i, f, b)
    fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
}

lesson.md: A **constant** is declared with `const`. Its value is fixed and can never change. The operator `+` adds numbers and also joins strings.

lesson.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    const greeting = "Welcome"
    const maxUsers = 100
    message := greeting + ", Ana"
    fmt.Println(message)
    fmt.Println(maxUsers * 2)
}

lesson.md: Go never mixes types by itself. To convert, write the type like a function: `float64(n)` or `int(x)`. Dividing two `int` values gives an `int`, so `7 / 2` is `3`. `int(1.99)` cuts off the decimals and gives `1`.

lesson.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    total := 7
    parts := 2
    fmt.Println(total / parts)
    fmt.Println(float64(total) / float64(parts))
    height := 1.99
    fmt.Println(int(height))
}

card: `x := 5` declares a variable and sets it
`var s string` gets the zero value `""`

units.title: Control flow
units.summary: Make decisions with if and switch, and repeat code with the different forms of the for loop.

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. Go needs no parentheses around the condition, but the braces are required. You compare with `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`, and combine conditions with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not).

An `if` can start with a short statement, followed by a semicolon. A variable created there exists only inside the `if` and its `else` branches. The operator `%` gives the rest of a division, so `n%2 == 0` checks for an even number.
Go has only one loop keyword: `for`. The classic form has three parts: a start statement, a condition and a statement that runs after each round.
With only a condition, `for` repeats while the condition is `true`. Other languages call this a while loop. `for { }` without a condition repeats forever, until a `break`.
`for i := range 6` counts from `0` to `5`. `continue` jumps to the next round, and `break` ends the loop at once.

`switch` compares a value with several cases and runs the first one that matches. A case can list several values. Go stops after the matching case, so you need no `break`. `default` runs when no case matches. A `switch` without a value checks conditions, like a chain of `if` and `else if`.

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions with parameters, return one or more values, and accept any number of arguments.

lesson.md: A **function** gives a piece of code a name. You define it with `func`, outside of `main`, and call it by its name. Each parameter has a name followed by its type.
The result type comes after the parentheses. `return` sends a value back to the caller. When parameters share a type, you write it once: `a, b int`.
Arguments must match the parameter types exactly. `add(2.5, 1)` does not compile, because `add` expects `int` values.
A Go function can return several values. List their types in parentheses. The caller receives them with `q, r := divide(17, 5)`. The blank name `_` throws away a value you do not need.
The order of functions in a file does not matter. You can define `divide` below `main` and still call it from `main`.

A **variadic** function accepts any number of values. Write `...` before the type of the last parameter. Inside the function, `nums` holds all the values, and `for _, n := range nums` visits each one. You learn more about this in the next world.
You already know a variadic function: `fmt.Println` accepts any number of values. That is why `fmt.Println(1, "a", true)` works.

card: `func add(a, b int) int { return a + b }`
`func sum(nums ...int)` takes any number of ints

units.title: Slices and maps
units.summary: Keep many values in arrays, slices and maps: add, read, loop over and delete elements.

lesson.md: An **array** has a fixed length that is part of its type: `[3]int` holds exactly three `int` values. A **slice** like `[]string` has no fixed length and can grow. You read an element by its index, and the first index is `0`. `len` gives the number of elements.
`append` adds values to a slice and returns the new slice, so you assign the result back. `s[1:3]` takes the elements from index `1` up to, but not including, index `3`.

lesson.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var names []string
    names = append(names, "Ada")
    names = append(names, "Bob", "Cy")
    fmt.Println(names, len(names))
    fmt.Println(names[1:3])
}

lesson.md: An index that does not exist stops the program with a **panic** (a run-time error). With three elements, `names[3]` panics, because the last index is `2`.
`for i, v := range s` visits every element: `i` is the index and `v` the value. Write `_` instead of `i` when you do not need the index.
A **map** stores pairs of keys and values. `map[string]int` has `string` keys and `int` values. `m[key] = value` adds a pair or changes it, `delete(m, key)` removes it, and `len(m)` counts the pairs.

`make(map[string]int)` creates an empty map. Reading a missing key gives the zero value. To find out if a key exists, read two values: `v, ok := m[key]`. `ok` is `true` only when the key is in the map.

`for k, v := range m` loops over a map, but the order changes from run to run. `fmt.Println` prints maps with sorted keys. A map declared with `var m map[string]int` is `nil`, and writing to it panics, so create maps with `make` or `{}`.

card: `v, ok := m[key]` checks if a key exists

units.title: Structs and methods
units.summary: Group data in your own struct types and add methods with value and pointer receivers.

lesson.md: A **struct** groups several values, called **fields**, into one new type. You define it with `type Name struct { ... }`, create a value with `Book{Title: "Go Basics", Pages: 120}` and reach a field with a dot: `b.Title`. The verb `%+v` prints a struct with its field names.
Fields that you do not set get their zero value. Fields of the same type can share one line: `X, Y int`.
A **method** is a function that belongs to a type. It has a **receiver** in parentheses before its name: `func (r Rect) Area() float64`. You call it with a dot: `r.Area()`.

A **value receiver** like `(c Counter)` gets a copy, so its changes are lost. A **pointer receiver** like `(c *Counter)` works on the original value and can change it. When you call `c.Inc()` on a variable, Go passes the pointer for you.
`&` gives the address of a value, which is a **pointer**. `&Player{Name: "Ana"}` has the type `*Player`. You use the same dot to reach fields and methods through a pointer.
A good rule: use a pointer receiver when the method changes the struct. If one method of a type needs a pointer receiver, give all its methods pointer receivers.

units.title: Interfaces
units.summary: Describe behavior with interfaces, make your types printable with fmt.Stringer and check types with a type switch.

lesson.md: An **interface** is a list of methods. Every type that has these methods satisfies the interface automatically. There is no `implements` keyword. A slice of an interface type can hold values of different types.
A function with an interface parameter accepts every type that satisfies the interface. The function only uses the methods of the interface.
A method with a pointer receiver belongs to the pointer type only. If `Speak` had the receiver `*Dog`, then `&Dog{}` would satisfy `Speaker`, but `Dog{}` would not.

The `fmt` package defines the interface `fmt.Stringer` with one method: `String() string`. When your type has this method, `fmt.Println` and `%v` use it. `fmt.Sprintf` works like `Printf`, but it returns the text instead of printing it.
The type `any` has no methods, so it can hold a value of any type. A **type switch** `switch v := x.(type)` checks which type the value really has. Inside each case, `v` has the type of that case.

lesson.output:
int 42
string hi
bool
other float64

lesson.md: To check for one single type, use a **type assertion** with two results: `s, ok := x.(string)`. If `x` holds a `string`, `ok` is `true`. Otherwise `ok` is `false` and `s` gets the zero value.

lesson.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var x any = "hello"
    s, ok := x.(string)
    fmt.Println(s, ok)
    n, ok := x.(int)
    fmt.Println(n, ok)
}

lesson.md: Keep interfaces small. Many useful interfaces in Go have only one method, like `fmt.Stringer`.

card: A type satisfies an interface by having its methods (no `implements`)
`s, ok := x.(string)` is a type assertion

units.title: Errors
units.summary: Handle errors the Go way: check if err != nil, create errors with errors.New and fmt.Errorf, and return them.

lesson.md: In Go an error is a normal value of the type `error`. A function that can fail returns an `error` as its **last** result. The value `nil` means that there was no error. `strconv.Atoi` converts text to an `int` and returns such an error.
Check the error right after the call with `if err != nil`. Handle the problem there, for example with `continue` or `return`. The normal code continues after the `if`.
When `err` is not `nil`, the other results usually hold zero values. Do not use them before you have checked the error.

`errors.New` creates an error with a fixed message. Your function returns it as the last value, and returns `nil` when everything works. Error messages start with a lowercase letter and have no period at the end.
`fmt.Errorf` builds the message with verbs, like `fmt.Sprintf`, and returns an `error`.

Often a function cannot fix an error itself. It returns the error to its caller and adds context with the verb `%w`, which wraps the original error. `errors.Is(err, target)` checks if `err` is `target` or wraps it.
